section.t: The cryptographic basis is: chain hashing for integrity within the record; owner signatures over position and effect for every change of power; type-specific session signatures; re-derivation of non-migrated admissions and CORE/BUDGET refusals on replay, while CONNECTOR, reconciliation and external-decider findings remain signer claims; and, for freshness, owner-attested heads held outside the host.

section.name: The host is trusted by the engine, not by the verifier
section.t: The engine runs inside the host with the host's permissions; a host can skip the check, patch the clock or read key files. The model confines what the host can do undetected rather than pretend otherwise. Unhooked calls are not seen (); a verifier assessing a completeness claim MUST obtain and report the coverage table. A decision is point-in-time. History time is the writers' claim: a clock set forward expires grants early, a clock set backward is caught only when it would precede the head. Deployments SHOULD use a monotone, trusted clock, readers SHOULD refuse a head unreasonably ahead of their own clock, and where grants and budgets depend on time a deployment SHOULD identify a trusted-time or witness-receipt-time binding and its uncertainty. A single signer's control over time is bounded only as states. A session key has similar control. A session record carries a timestamp chosen by its signer. Replay rejects it if that time is at or past the session's expiry, and, under the attested floor, at or past the expiry of an owner attestation that was still valid at the preceding head (). Someone who steals a session key and can add records directly can therefore move history time forward to just before the earlier of those limits. Advancing the epoch stops further records but does not move time back. Deployments SHOULD accept session records only through their own writer, which checks each timestamp against the deployment's trusted clock; a verifier cannot tell afterwards whether that writer was used. A history whose genesis sets a session-time horizon () bounds this in replay itself: a session key can then move history time no further than that horizon past the time of the latest owner-signed record that advanced history time. The cost is operational: once the horizon is reached, sessions cannot record until an owner writes such a record, so an unattended deployment needs scheduled owner records and therefore an owner key that is available.

section.t: A key used under this model SHOULD sign only domain-separated challenges defined by its profile, so that it cannot serve as a signing oracle for another protocol. Distinct committed keys SHOULD be held by distinct custodians; profiles SHOULD require finite session expiry outside migrated prefixes; and the incident procedure SHOULD review the compromise interval, append revocations and advance epochs. FROST or another threshold scheme may produce an ordinary profile-valid signature; that is distinct from a policy requiring separate signatures by several enrolled keys. A deployment with more than one human key SHOULD require at least two signatures for a key rotation, and with a threshold of two or more SHOULD set the power-reducing types to one so that one present human can always stop an agent. Uninstall, upgrade and file-deletion restrictions are operating-system controls, not consequences of the signature scheme.

section.name: Rollback, refusals, delegation, availability, claims
section.t: Rollback. Without evidence outside the host, a rollback to any head the owner once attested is undetectable. A reachable witness bound to the history closes this; what remains is a copy from before the first binding, the window while the witness is unreachable, the administrator of both host and witness, and the records after the last witnessed head. A deployment MUST state which apply. Anchors and committee checkpoints add known-head evidence; a fresh reader needs an authenticated bootstrap; a hidden fork remains hidden.

Unsigned records and refusals. Only control records carry an owner signature; a party who can write the file but holds no admitted session cannot add admissions, refusals or observations. Instantiations SHOULD sign intent declarations, so that a file writer cannot squat identifiers. A denied agent cannot fill the history with refusals: they are session-signed, coalesced and rate-limited, bounded by declared capacity that never refuses power-reducing controls, and a CORE or budget refusal the state would have allowed is rejected on replay. CONNECTOR claims can still be false.

Delegation and prohibition. Attenuation is a replay rule, prohibition scope and path selection decide what is overridden, and required intersections need live partners; these three let a verifier bound the maximum authority any actor could have had from the history alone. Retiring a counterparty does not deny consequential requests that name it; stop them with a prohibition, a budget or at the connector. A proof-size refusal is not a denial of authority: a power-reducing revocation or termination can remove an oversized winning path and let a smaller granted path produce a proof, turning that refusal into an ALLOW. To stop an actor, use a prohibition, a zero-cap budget, a fence or a termination, never a proof-size limit.

Availability. Declared capacity preserves withdrawal; absolute caps, disk failure, a stale lock or signer failure can still stop revocation and termination, so an independent executor stop channel is a deployment requirement where safety depends on withdrawal. Deployments MUST plan for a history's terminal state and a successor, MUST choose and document whether a witness outage stops gated owner writes or permits them up to a bound, and must keep a separate emergency stop boundary when effects are finality-gated.

Receipts and outcomes are local claims. A receipt establishes that a session signed a claim at a head; an effect, that a measurer reported a quantity; an outcome, that an attester reported a status. Deployments MUST NOT describe a history as proof of what an agent did, as opposed to what the decision point saw and decided and what signers claimed.

Cryptographic agility. The model names no mandatory algorithm. An instantiation MUST specify its hash, signature suites and canonical encoding, MUST bind the suite to each key when the key is declared, and SHOULD require strict signature verification (for Ed25519 : canonical encodings, no small-order keys, cofactorless verification).

section.name: Privacy Considerations
section.t: A history records who was allowed to do what, who was refused and who owes what; it is not confidential by construction. Deployments SHOULD keep secrets out of identifiers and descriptions, SHOULD commit to terms by digest and hold content elsewhere, and SHOULD limit disclosure and retention. Encryption requires a profile defining what is committed and how auditors recover it. The model provides no erasure: a record needed for replay cannot be removed, so identifiers that must later be erasable SHOULD be pseudonymous or held outside the history under a salted commitment. Observation call fields, effects and counterparty receipts import third-party data into the history and SHOULD be minimized to what matching and verification need. Query answers MAY withhold fields under a disclosure policy; that policy does not protect the file. Refusal records deserve particular care, since they record what a person's agent attempted and was denied; access to them SHOULD be governed at least as strictly as access to admissions.

A witness or transparency service learns that a history existed and advanced at given times; the witness design exposes only genesis, rotations and head hashes, while registration of records exposes their content unless by hash, and even hash-only registration reveals cadence. Unsalted hashes of low-entropy names permit guessing. Public anchors reveal publication cadence, account and commitment metadata; the persistence tier makes the history public. Cross-history correlation is possible wherever an identifier recurs; deployments that need unlinkability SHOULD use pairwise identifiers and SHOULD avoid registering raw identifiers with a shared service. Selective disclosure cannot remove transitions needed for replay, and a redacted view must state which conclusions remain verifiable.

A PHL attestation profile should retain only minimal signed verification and vouching facts, keeping biometric templates and media out of the history and registry. Device identifiers and vouch graphs can still reveal identities and relationships; a digest is not anonymization, and hashes alone MUST NOT be described as anonymity. Optional proofs keep the public-statement and aggregate-release limits of : computing an aggregate correctly does not establish unbiased enrollment, and a private lineage predicate does not establish physical humanity beyond its evidence policy. RFC 6973 describes the correlation and identification threats that apply.

section.name: IANA Considerations
section.t: This document has no IANA actions. A future wire profile may register media types for exports and head statements, and COSE header parameters or CBOR Web Token (CWT) claims for the SCITT mapping; those registrations belong to the profile.

front.title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels

abstract.t: In many standards track documents several words are used to signify the requirements in the specification. These words are often capitalized. This document defines these words as they should be interpreted in IETF documents. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

front.title: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words

abstract.t: RFC 2119 specifies common key words that may be used in protocol specifications. This document aims to reduce the ambiguity by clarifying that only UPPERCASE usage of the key words have the defined special meanings.

front.title: An Architecture for Trustworthy and Transparent Digital Supply Chains

abstract.t: Traceability in supply chains is a growing security concern. While Verifiable Data Structures (VDSs) have addressed specific issues, such as equivocation over digital certificates, they lack a universal architecture for all supply chains. This document defines such an architecture for single-issuer signed statement transparency. It ensures extensibility and interoperability between different transparency services as well as compliance with various auditing procedures and regulatory requirements.

front.title: Improving Awareness of Running Code: The Implementation Status Section

abstract.t: This document describes a simple process that allows authors of Internet-Drafts to record the status of known implementations by including an Implementation Status section. This will allow reviewers and working groups to assign due consideration to documents that have the benefit of running code, which may serve as evidence of valuable experimentation and feedback that have made the implemented protocols more mature.

This process is not mandatory. Authors of Internet-Drafts are encouraged to consider using the process for their documents, and working groups are invited to think about applying the process to all of their protocol specifications. This document obsoletes RFC 6982, advancing it to a Best Current Practice.

front.title: Certificate Transparency

abstract.t: This document describes an experimental protocol for publicly logging the existence of Transport Layer Security (TLS) certificates as they are issued or observed, in a manner that allows anyone to audit certificate authority (CA) activity and notice the issuance of suspect certificates as well as to audit the certificate logs themselves. The intent is that eventually clients would refuse to honor certificates that do not appear in a log, effectively forcing CAs to add all issued certificates to the logs.
Logs are network services that implement the protocol operations for submissions and queries that are defined in this document.

front.title: Certificate Transparency Version 2.0

abstract.t: This document describes version 2.0 of the Certificate Transparency (CT) protocol for publicly logging the existence of Transport Layer Security (TLS) server certificates as they are issued or observed, in a manner that allows anyone to audit certification authority (CA) activity and notice the issuance of suspect certificates as well as to audit the certificate logs themselves. The intent is that eventually clients would refuse to honor certificates that do not appear in a log, effectively forcing CAs to add all issued certificates to the logs.
This document obsoletes RFC 6962. It also specifies a new TLS extension that is used to send various CT log artifacts.
Logs are network services that implement the protocol operations for submissions and queries that are defined in this document.

front.title: Edwards-Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA)

abstract.t: This document describes elliptic curve signature scheme Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA). The algorithm is instantiated with recommended parameters for the edwards25519 and edwards448 curves. An example implementation and test vectors are provided.

front.title: OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange

abstract.t: This specification defines a protocol for an HTTP- and JSON-based Security Token Service (STS) by defining how to request and obtain security tokens from OAuth 2.0 authorization servers, including security tokens employing impersonation and delegation.

front.title: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE): Structures and Process

abstract.t: Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) is a data format designed for small code size and small message size. There is a need to be able to define basic security services for this data format. This document defines the CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) protocol. This specification describes how to create and process signatures, message authentication codes, and encryption using CBOR for serialization. This specification additionally describes how to represent cryptographic keys using CBOR.
This document, along with RFC 9053, obsoletes RFC 8152.

front.title: Remote ATtestation procedureS (RATS) Architecture

abstract.t: In network protocol exchanges, it is often useful for one end of a communication to know whether the other end is in an intended operating state. This document provides an architectural overview of the entities involved that make such tests possible through the process of generating, conveying, and evaluating evidentiary Claims. It provides a model that is neutral toward processor architectures, the content of Claims, and protocols.

front.title: The Flexible Round-Optimized Schnorr Threshold (FROST) Protocol for Two-Round Schnorr Signatures

abstract.t: This document specifies the Flexible Round-Optimized Schnorr Threshold (FROST) signing protocol. FROST signatures can be issued after a threshold number of entities cooperate to compute a signature, allowing for improved distribution of trust and redundancy with respect to a secret key. FROST depends only on a prime-order group and cryptographic hash function. This document specifies a number of ciphersuites to instantiate FROST using different prime-order groups and hash functions. This document is a product of the Crypto Forum Research Group (CFRG) in the IRTF.

front.title: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) Receipts

abstract.t: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) Receipts prove properties of a Verifiable Data Structure (VDS) to a verifier. VDSs and associated Proof Types enable security properties, such as minimal disclosure, transparency, and non-equivocation. Transparency helps maintain trust over time and has been applied to certificates, end-to-end encrypted messaging systems, and supply chain security. This specification enables concise transparency-oriented systems by building on Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) and COSE. The extensibility of the approach is demonstrated by providing CBOR encodings for Merkle inclusion and consistency proofs.

section.name: Example encoding: an append-only JSON Lines history
section.t: This appendix is informative. It describes the "format 2" history of the IronTrellis implementation, to show that the model is implementable and to fix vocabulary. Format 2 was released with the first public release candidate; later rule changes are a new format, and format-2 histories keep their verdicts. Nothing here is normative for the model.

section.name: Store, chain and state
section.t: A history is a UTF-8 file with one JSON object per line: a version literal, the previous record hash, the event {id, type, timestamp, data} with data canonically encoded (keys in UTF-8 byte order, integers only, amounts as decimal strings), and the line's own record hash:

with prev thirty-two zero bytes at p = 0. The head is {hash, position, canonicalTime} and recordHash(0) identifies the history. After every event the state is a sorted set of closed records (event, genesis, owner key epoch, principal, agent, role, tenure, succession, session, authority, usage, nonce, intent, receipt, obligation, duty, anchor, witness binding and policy, budget, counterparty, refusal, effect, observation, reconciliation cursor); leaves are SHA-256(0x00 || kind || 0x00 || key || 0x00 || SHA-256(canonical(record))) sorted by (kind, key), and the root follows 's recursion. A checkpoint at c commits to the state after c-1.

Optional distinct-key policies add a global threshold, per-type thresholds, agent and human classes, pre-event quorum checks and a second authorization container excluded from the effect hash; a history without these fields replays unchanged. Session events carry {runtimeSessionId, credentialKeyId, controlEpoch} and a type-specific challenge; admissions sign the decision-time challenge of .

section.name: Refusals, duties, export, witness
section.t: A refusal is REQUEST_REFUSED with refusalSource CORE, BUDGET or CONNECTOR, the request, evaluationTime, expectedHistoryHead, decision, code, optional budgetId or connector: {connectorId, refusalCode, detailDigest}, the session binding and refusalAuthorization. Replay re-runs CORE and BUDGET refusals and rejects the event with REFUSAL_NOT_REPRODUCED on any difference; a CONNECTOR refusal carries CONNECTOR_REFUSED. A handover is the operation succeed: AGENT_TERMINATED then ROLE_TRANSFERRED, sealed by a STATE_CHECKPOINT, with a report listing open duties, live grants each marked as not following, sessions, tenures and the SURVIVES answer.

The export view irontrellis-export/2 carries the domain, genesis hash, heads, roots and counts at both ends of a range, every event with its hashes, checkpoints, optional full record sets, requested inclusion paths, every rotation at or before the end, held attestations and the complete earlier-body dependency closure. Type 42 RECONCILIATION_OBSERVED carries the observation fields of under the challenge irontrellis-reconciliation-authorization/2; its error order is schema, session and fence, reconciler binding, preceding head, match, duplicate or equivocation, uniqueness, capacity.

The witness protocol irontrellis-witness/1 keeps per history a chain of statements {version, historyId, domain, head, previous | null}, accepted only if signed by a key in force at the head and previous is the witness's latest. Entries (REGISTERED, HEAD, ROTATED, EQUIVOCATION, SUPERSEDED) are leaves of an tree with proofs; checkpoints are signed notes; every latest-head answer is signed over a client nonce. The anchor statement for the public-chain tier, irontrellis-anchor-statement/1, has a frozen field list and canonical rule; its first vector (1,076 bytes, chain eip155:42793) has been reproduced independently.

section.name: Implementation status
section.t: This appendix is informative, in the spirit of , and reports documentary evidence as of 29 October 2026. It is not a certification of conformance. The IronTrellis implementation was released as open source on 29 October 2026, as the release candidate 1.0.0-rc.2 . The release tag is signed with a hardware-held key, and the eleven npm packages built from it were published by the repository's release workflow with provenance statements linking each package to that build; the downloads, checksums and documents are listed with the release . It connects to coding agents through hooks for Claude Code, OpenAI Codex CLI and Cursor, and to agent frameworks through shims for the OpenAI Agents SDK and LangGraph; the repository's quick start is the easiest way to try the model.

The implementation pairs this model with two operational documents. A commissioning disclosure , which every party commissioning an installation reads and signs, states each critical failure mode (time base, anchoring, witnesses, key custody, host compromise, unhooked paths, the limits of replay, federation, privacy and outages) in three parts: what can go wrong, what the implementation does about it, and what the installation itself must do. Where a duty could fall between the two, it is named on both sides, and protections the current release does not yet provide are marked as such. An install checklist turns these duties into steps for a single experimenter and for an organisation, with an optional external review before commissioning. Both are informative; this document does not require them.

section.t: On 29 October 2026 the reference writer's test suite passed on a Linux host for the release commit: 1,810 tests, 1,797 passing, none failing, and 13 skipped because they need a secrets service, administrator rights or an earlier release build that the host did not provide. On the repository's hosted Linux runners the same suite passed under Node.js 22 and 24, and the published irontrellis package ran its demo on a clean host. The hosted macOS and Windows jobs did not pass for this release; Windows is not yet a supported platform. Running the suite on faster hosted runners before the release found a race in the coding-agent hook: two copies of the hook deciding the same call could refer it to the user instead of refusing it, because one read the clock before the other's refusal was recorded; the hook never allowed such a call on its own. It was fixed before the release tag, with regression tests. One engine defect, in the encoding of a succession record, was found by a separate conformance exercise; it has been fixed, with regression tests. The TypeScript verifier shares code with the writer and is not independent of it; the Python checker is advisory and is not a writer. In the one checker comparison that found disagreements, all seven were the checker lagging rulings already in force. No external cryptographic audit is claimed.

Public-chain anchoring. The release candidate does not itself verify chain anchors: its anchor check produces no report and lists chain inclusion and finality as missing evidence. Separate tools in its repository record histories on Etherlink Shadownet (chain 127823) under a test profile, and on 25 October 2026 they recorded a first worked history on Etherlink mainnet (chain 42793); those tools report finality in TRUSTED_NODE mode, from nodes the operator chose (). Anchoring in CONSENSUS_VERIFIED mode, which needs an independently administered, validating Tezos node to confirm finality, is defined and partly vectored, and is not part of this release candidate; when it comes, it adds to these records rather than correcting them.

Zero-knowledge proofs. Seven zero-knowledge proofs are published with the release as a demonstration , one for each of the seven synthetic workloads (revocation, three-period, count, cumulative, exhaustion, handover of both, handover of state). They were produced on 29 October 2026 with a pinned build of the implementation's segmented proof program, made on Linux, on synthetic histories; rebuilding that program byte for byte from published source is future work (below). The download holds the root proofs, the root verification key, the proof program with its configuration, and a small verifier that can be built from the public OpenVM source. Before publication, two verifiers built and run separately, one written independently against the published OpenVM library, accepted all seven and refused tampered copies, and the program's commitments and verification key were regenerated from the published program and configuration and matched. Each proof shows only that the program's checks passed for one small synthetic history, within the rules the program supports; the proofs are not production-qualified, whether the program implements this model faithfully is under review, and they establish neither authority, completeness nor freshness. A research experiment produced and verified Groth16/BN254 proofs of hidden principal-record membership under an actual format-2 state root (arkworks 0.5.0, single-party setup, eight-event fixture), with signatures and replay outside the circuit. In October 2026 an earlier edition of the implementation's segmented proof program was also proved on seven synthetic workloads; that program followed an earlier edition of the rules and could not be rebuilt byte for byte on Linux, so those proofs are not published. A larger proof run is in progress and has not yet completed.

section.name: Formal verification: what was chosen, what it proves, what it does not
section.t: This appendix is informative. IronTrellis does not model every path through the implementation; it chose the paths where a mistake would hurt most and wrote each as a model in Lean 4, stating properties the model must satisfy and letting the kernel check them. lists each path, and explains the choices for a general reader. A selection of these proofs is published with the release : a self-contained Lean project of 32 source files and 15 headline theorems covering the decision procedure, revocation, owner keys and attestation, spending accounting, committees and anchoring, with each theorem's exact premises and the commands that rebuild them and print the axioms each one relies on. Every result listed passed under one gate: Lean 4.34.1 with core and Std only, no sorry, admit, native_decide or custom axioms, with #print axioms recorded for every theorem. The integrated edition of 17 October 2026 (186 modules, 2,048 theorems) was rebuilt from source on separate hardware with an independently installed Lean, and every theorem in it depends only on Lean's three standard axioms. A rebuild checks the proofs, not whether each model states the rules faithfully; that is reviewed separately. The models are being brought up to the current edition of the rules: the 17 October edition predates the optional session-time horizon (), so its results hold for histories that set none.

A model of path selection, attenuation, intersections, prohibitions and caps; the model and the engine agree on 120,000 generated cases. Revocation is monotone at the authority-verdict stage: revoking a permission never turns a request that was not allowed into one that is allowed, before the proof-size preflight. This is proved for the executable procedure model under a valid record set, when no unrevoked prohibition has the revoked permission in its ancestry (the revocation entries of ), and rebuilt independently; terminating an agent is proved likewise
A model of the rules, not the code; agreement on cases is evidence, not proof. Monotonicity of the final verdict is not claimed: the proof-size preflight can still differ ()

section.t: What the proofs caught. A signed twelve-event history in which revoking a grant turned a clear DENY into an ALLOW, because the engine checked a cumulative cap after choosing a path; the rule was moved. A single-signature termination of an agent in the middle of a delegation chain that would have silently switched off a prohibition depending on it; the rule was tightened. A null-expiry session from a migrated prefix that could still attest a duty finding; the rule now expires it. Two liveness promises of the "you can always do X" kind that were false in edge cases, such as a policy where one key is enough.

What they do not show. The proofs are about models of the rules, not the TypeScript that runs; the two are connected by testing on large case sets, which is strong evidence, not proof. Cryptography is assumed: signatures cannot be forged and hashes do not collide. A proof shows exactly the statement written down. Some results hold only under named assumptions, and each is listed. Nothing shows that a person meant to approve something or that a report from the world is true. The largest open piece is a proof that replaying any history always rebuilds exactly the same state.

Where this is going. Each rule change is followed by re-checking the proofs it touches. The selection published with the release rebuilds with two commands, so that a reader can rerun it rather than take this appendix's word; the full editions, a claims ledger naming every theorem with its assumptions and exclusions, the counterexamples that changed rules, and the scripts that compare the models with the engine are to follow in the same way. The zero-knowledge demonstration of is to be completed the same way: the source of the proof program with a pinned recipe for rebuilding it, the EVM verifier contract and its proof, and the questions and results for each synthetic history.

section.name: Relation to other work
section.t: Signed Permissions and Action Receipts (, revision -01) specifies passkey permissions, attenuating delegation, signed action receipts, acknowledged cancellation and signed tree heads, and maps its records onto the AUDIT architecture's record types; its verifier separates malformed evidence from sound records reporting actions outside permission, whereas this model rejects admissions that do not reproduce ALLOW. Replayed actor, session and epoch state, role tenures and surviving duties are not specified there. Neither design proves complete execution history from agent-generated records alone.

AUDIT (, revision -01) organizes cross-domain record generation, audit context and auditing services, including delegation and authorization transition records, and keeps real-time enforcement outside its post-hoc scope. This document supplies a proposed state-transition component; duties and reconciliation are proposals for discussion, not adopted work items.

OAuth and WIMSE. Token exchange and transaction tokens carry delegation inside tokens for a request; the WIMSE architecture gives workloads identifiers and short-lived credentials. A session admission can bind a WIMSE credential's key, a grant can be the authority behind a token issuance, and a token's claims can reference the grant identifier; the record of authority is the history, the token a derived credential whose issuance and revocation can themselves be recorded.
RATS can establish properties of the environment that produced a record; this model carries evidence references for that purpose and does not define attestation.

Human delegation provenance () describes session-bound human authorization and a signed delegation chain with optional proof-of-humanity credentials. Overlapping concerns do not imply wire interoperability or identical assurance.

section.name: SCITT mapping
section.t: This mapping is informative. Registering IronTrellis signatures does not automatically create SCITT Signed Statements or Receipts. A future profile could wrap an owner head attestation, export digest, control record or session claim in a newly signed COSE_Sign1 statement , defining payload canonicalization, issuer identity and key discovery; reusing a raw signature as a COSE signature is invalid because the signing inputs differ. SCITT requires protected iss and sub claims on statements and Receipts ; a profile could scope the subject to a history identity. The witness evidence of is analogous but has no compliant COSE mapping. Registration does not establish statement truth or issuer completeness, and submitted-head chaining cannot detect an unsubmitted suffix.

section.name: Worked model example
section.t: This informative sequence is illustrative, not a conformance fixture.

list.t: An authenticated owner creates two agents and an exclusive purchasing role, admits their sessions, and declares a succession rule. Only the current agent receives a bounded purchasing grant.

A purchase is admitted under the current head. A separately signed counterparty report is recorded. An uncertain submission preserves its original identity and allowance; the replacement may observe its result but does not dispatch it again.

A request exceeding a grant or budget produces a reproduced refusal. A supplied provider event is separately recorded as MATCHED or UNMATCHED; matching the refusal does not authorize the reported call.

An investigation duty remains attached to the role. Handover terminates the predecessor, transfers the tenure and reports surviving work and non-transferring grants. The successor needs fresh authority for performance assignment, resource restoration and disposition.
A prospective policy permits a purpose-bound finding and authorized disposition. A contest remains visible. Segmented continuation preserves the same genesis, usage, pending identity and duties.

An auditor authenticates the intended history and export boundaries, replays the range with its dependencies, and reports authority, claims, inclusion, freshness and outcome assurance separately. An optional hidden-record proof establishes only its pinned predicate.
